[PolicyMap][policymap] has published an interesting article titled *"[A deeper 
look at gerrymandering][article]"* on their blog as part of a three-part series. 
The article is an explainer on redistricting, set strictly in the political 
context of the USA (hence: gerrymandering[^gerrymandering]): 

> Packing concentrates a group’s voters into as few districts as possible. Those 
districts are won overwhelmingly, every vote beyond what was needed to win is 
wasted, and the group’s influence everywhere else drops accordingly.
> 
> Cracking does the reverse: it splits a group across many districts so that it 
constitutes a majority in none of them.

I find this interesting not so much because of the theoretical underpinnings 
(the MAUP[^maup]) and the redistricting / gerrymandering mechanics, but because 
this article invites a cold, hard look in the mirror with regard to our 
discipline, the concepts, the methods and the tools it produces and their 
ethical implications – whether or not you care about this specific context.

[article]: https://www.policymap.com/blog/a-deeper-look-at-gerrymandering
[policymap]: https://www.policymap.com/

[^gerrymandering]: The manipulation of electoral district boundaries to favour 
a party or group, typically by "packing" opposing voters into few districts or 
"cracking" them across many.
[^maup]: The [Modifiable Areal Unit Problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modifiable_areal_unit_problem): 
the results of aggregating spatial data depend on the scale and on how the 
boundaries of the areal units are drawn.
